new_statements.quote: On the phonological level, they all share a suprasegmental system which manifests itself in a complex stress system with rhythm principles, and in addition, the languages of the Kiwaian and Eastern Trans-Fly Families seem to possess a two-tone system with usually low to very low functional load. [...] [p. 334, of the Pahoturi River and Morehead and Upper Maro Rivers Families:] On the phonological level, all these languages appear to lack a tonal system.

new_statements.relation_note: Group-level only: stress-based prosody with rhythmic (alternating) patterns asserted for the whole stock; no tone in the Morehead-Upper Maro (Yam) group. No stress position, no data, no language-by-language detail for the Nambu Sub-Family; Namat not named.
new_statements.rule_in_words: All Trans-Fly Stock languages (incl. the Morehead-Upper Maro family with its Nambu Sub-Family) are said to have a 'complex stress system with rhythm principles' (no position stated); tone is reported only for the Kiwaian and Eastern Trans-Fly families, and the Pahoturi + Morehead-Upper Maro group is said to lack a tonal system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'rhythm principles' implies rhythmic secondary prominence but nothing specific is stated
new_statements.exceptions: none for the Nambu group; tone exceptions concern Kiwaian (absent in Wabuda, higher load in NE Kiwai/Arigibi) and Tirio (no tone)
new_statements.identity_note: Stock-level typological generalisation over the whole Trans-Fly Stock (1975 classification), whose 'Morehead and Upper Maro Rivers Family, Nambu Sub-Family' (listed as Nambu 800, Iauga/Parb 700, Dorro 75; p. 330) is the group Namat belongs to today (Yam, Nambu branch); Namat, Mibini and Potaia are never named, so the remark covers Namat only by group membership. Second-hand and impressionistic; not a first-hand Namat statement. | Wurm's 'Nambu' is a cover term for the whole Nambu dialect chain of the Morehead district; his village list opens with Mibini, which is the Namat [nkm] village (Rueck 2011; Yamfinder), alongside villages of today's Nama, Namo, Nambo, Neme etc. The typological notes come from Wurm's own 1966 fieldnotes on 'Nambu and Iauga (Parb)'; the village of his Nambu informants is not stated, so the statement is group-level for the chain that includes Namat rather than specifically about Mibini speech. [name in source: Nambu (villages Mibini, Garaita, Setavi, Mata, Saraina, Pongaki, Gubam, Keru, Derideri, Arufi, Tais); pages 152-154 (sec. 3.35.11)]

new_statements.quote: Nambu is spoken in the villages of Mibini, Garaita, Setavi (a Nambu-Upper Morehead bilingual village), Mata, Saraina, Pongaki (or Pangaraki), Gubam, Keru, Derideri, Arufi and Tais by a total of about 700 speakers. [...] The present writer has information from his own fieldnotes, on the structures of Nambu and Iauga (Parb) which are virtually identical. The following notes reflect only their features. The phonology is quite complex, and the following statements are also tentative. [...] Vowel length is phonemic. Several diphthongs are found. The suprasegmental system appears to consist of a relatively complex stress system with rhythm principles, but no tonal system seems to be present.

sources.note: About the sister language Nmbo [ncm], not Namat: impressionistic; 'it seems that stress falls on the first syllable for two- and three-syllable words'; stress attracted to the first syllable with an open vowel; stress shift under cliticisation (sec. 4 'Prosody'). Namat not mentioned.

sources.citation: Carroll, Matthew J., Wolfgang Barth, Nicholas Evans, I Wayan Arka, Christian Doehler, Eri Kashima, Volker Gast, Tina Gregor, Kate L. Lindsey, Julia Miller, Emil Mittag, Bruno Olsson, Dineke Schokkin, Jeff Siegel, Charlotte van Tongeren & Kyla Quinn. 2024. CLDF dataset derived from 'Yamfinder: The Southern New Guinea Lexical Database', v1.0. Zenodo. doi:10.5281/zenodo.10843349 (github lexibank/yamfinder). Language 'namat' (nama1267, nkm): 417 forms, Village = Mibini, Source = js (Siegel, Jeff. Fieldwork data).
sources.note: No prose at all: 417 phonemic transcriptions (e.g. jənd, ʈarðær 'concept 4', mæmbə, ɸakərsok, kæŋgæt), Phonetic column empty, zero stress or pitch marks (no ˈ ˌ or accents), no comments. Wordlist-only data; shows segment inventory in use (retroflex ʈ, ð, ɸ, prenasalised stops, ə, æ) but nothing about prominence.

sources.citation: Evans, Nicholas. 2021. The phonetics of Southern New Guinea languages: an overview. In Kate L. Lindsey & Dineke Schokkin (eds.), Phonetic fieldwork in Southern New Guinea (LD&C Special Publication 24), ch. 1.
sources.note: Regional generalisation over eight languages (Yelmek, Ngkolmpu, Nmbo, Nen, Idi, Ende, Bitur, Urama), not Namat: 'it is difficult to identify any typological features of the phonologies of Southern New Guinea, other than absences (e.g., no tone, no pitch accent or distinctive stress except for Urama, no ejectives etc.)' (p. 7). Namat not mentioned.

sources.note: No phonology content. Section 2 'Sources and level of documentation' states that beyond Komnzo, Ngkolmpu, Ranmo, Nen and Nama the family has only word lists, and gives Evans et al. sources.note: Nmbo only. Namat is not named anywhere in the thesis; it says the Nambu branch is a dialect chain of at least six languages (Rueck 2006) plus Nä, Len, Ndre per Evans et al. 2018 (p. 48). No Namat stress information.

sources.citation: Usher, Timothy. n.d. [c. 2020-2024]. East Morehead River [Nambu family page, with Nama-Namat > Namat node]. New Guinea World (Santa Fe Institute / hosted at University of Zurich). Web resource.
sources.note: Nothing: no occurrence of stress, accent, tone, tonal or prosody. Gives a proto-East Morehead River consonant and vowel inventory (incl. retroflex series, labiovelars, diphthongs) and correspondence tables 'under construction'. Its value for Namat is the source inventory: Lyons (1913-1914: 193-194) 89-term Potoia vocabulary; Ray (1923: 337-338, 343) Potoia pronouns and numerals; Siegel (2015) Namat (Mibini) vocabulary in Carroll ed. 2015 (= Yamfinder); Tucker, Boevé, Fuller, Gustafsson & Rueck (2003) Nambu dialect survey 'unobtained'.

sources.citation: Rueck, Michael J. 2011. Social Network Analysis applied to language planning in the Morehead district, Papua New Guinea. SIL Electronic Survey Reports 2011-037. Dallas: SIL International (publication of the 2006 GIAL MA thesis).
sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic survey (lexicostatistics, social networks). Only Namat content: Namat = the speech variety of Mibini village (Table 3, p. 74; Table 19, p. 133); 'the two sets of dialects most likely to be willing to be grouped into a single language are Namna with Nambo and Namat with Nama.. during our visit to Mibini, people alternated between the names Namat and Nama when referring to their language (Tucker et al. 2003:38)' (pp. 132-133). No phonology, no wordlist printed, no stress.
